chapters.title: Identify where oxygen is bonded
chapters.formula: Alcohol: R-OH; ether: R-O-R'; aldehyde: R-CHO; ketone: R-CO-R'; acid: R-COOH
chapters.script: Welcome to Organic Oxygen. This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice. An alcohol has hydroxyl attached to a saturated carbon; a phenol has hydroxyl directly on an aromatic ring. An ether links two carbon groups through oxygen. An aldehyde has a carbonyl carbon attached to at least one hydrogen, whereas a ketone has two carbon substituents. A carboxylic acid contains a carbonyl and hydroxyl at the same carbon. Classify alcohols by the number of carbon groups attached to the carbon carrying hydroxyl, not by counting every hydroxyl in the molecule. Ethanol is primary, isopropyl alcohol secondary and tert butyl alcohol tertiary. This classification helps predict oxidation and dehydration, but the reagent still decides what reaction actually occurs. Compare ethanol with dimethyl ether: they share a molecular formula but differ in connectivity and hydrogen bonding. A carbonyl oxygen does not make a compound an alcohol, and two oxygens do not automatically make a carboxylic acid. Trace the bonds around the functional carbon. An ester has an oxygen bonded to a carbon group in place of the acid's hydroxyl hydrogen.
points: Alcohol · OH on saturated C · Ethanol
Phenol · OH on aromatic C · Phenol
Ketone · C=O; two C groups · Acetone

chapters.title: Oxidation and dehydration change different bonds
chapters.formula: CH3CH2OH -> CH3CHO -> CH3COOH: successive oxidation, with suitable reagents
chapters.script: A primary alcohol can oxidize to an aldehyde under suitable controlled conditions, or further to a carboxylic acid with stronger aqueous oxidation. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone. A tertiary alcohol lacks the hydrogen on its hydroxyl-bearing carbon needed for the usual direct oxidation; harsh oxidation may instead break carbon-carbon bonds. Acid-catalysed dehydration removes water to make an alkene. Protonating hydroxyl makes water a better leaving group. Secondary and tertiary substrates can involve carbocations and rearrangement; do not require a free primary carbocation for every primary alcohol. Heating ethanol with suitable acid can form ethene, while different temperatures and conditions can favour ether formation. For ethanol, controlled oxidation retains both carbons in acetaldehyde. Further oxidation gives acetic acid without adding another carbon. Reducing acetone instead gives isopropyl alcohol, the reverse functional group change of secondary alcohol oxidation. In dehydration the oxygen leaves as part of water, so oxygen accounting differs from oxidation. Compare products by both atom inventory and functional group rather than by the word heating alone.
points: Primary alcohol · Aldehyde → acid · Retained
Secondary alcohol · Ketone · Retained
Tertiary alcohol · No usual direct route · Harsh cleavage possible

chapters.title: Phenol acidity follows conjugate-base stabilization
chapters.formula: Typical acidity: carboxylic acid > phenol > simple alcohol, under comparable conditions
chapters.script: Phenol is more acidic than an ordinary alcohol because the phenoxide conjugate base benefits from resonance delocalization. Carboxylate ions share negative charge over two oxygens and are generally more stabilized still. These are comparisons under comparable conditions, not permission to apply one acidity ranking to every substituted molecule. Phenol reacts with aqueous hydroxide to form phenoxide but ordinarily does not release carbon dioxide from bicarbonate as a carboxylic acid does. Its hydroxyl group activates the ring and directs electrophilic substitution towards ortho and para sites. Bromine water can give 2,4,6-tribromophenol; controlled nitration can give ortho/para products. Reimer-Tiemann formylation gives an ortho-hydroxy aldehyde as the usual major product after work-up. Substituents can change these comparisons. An electron withdrawing group can stabilize phenoxide and increase phenol acidity, while its position affects resonance participation. The phenolic proton is not the same as a hydrogen attached to ring carbon. In Reimer Tiemann chemistry, a new carbon is added to the ring as part of an aldehyde group. Count seven carbons in the usual salicylaldehyde product compared with six in phenol.
points: Carboxylic acid · Reacts with HCO₃⁻ · Stabilized carboxylate
Phenol · Reacts with OH⁻ · Phenoxide resonance
Simple alcohol · Weaker acid · Less stabilized anion

chapters.title: Carbonyl carbon is an electrophilic target
chapters.formula: Carbonyl addition: nucleophile attacks C; C=O pi electrons move towards O
chapters.script: The carbon oxygen double bond is polarized, making carbon electron deficient. A nucleophile forms a bond to carbon while the pi electron pair moves towards oxygen, producing a tetrahedral intermediate. Proton transfer then gives the appropriate product. Simple aldehydes are often more reactive than comparable ketones because they have less crowding and less electron donation from alkyl groups. Cyanide addition followed by protonation gives a cyanohydrin under suitable conditions. Hydroxylamine can form an oxime, and suitable ammonia derivatives form other carbonyl derivatives through addition followed by water loss. A Grignard reagent adds a carbon group and, after acidic work-up, gives an alcohol. Acidic protons or moisture can quench it before this addition. A trigonal planar carbonyl carbon becomes tetrahedral during addition. If the final carbon has four different substituents, a new stereogenic centre may result. Under ordinary achiral conditions, attack on either face can give enantiomeric products rather than one guaranteed pure stereoisomer. This geometric consequence is separate from whether an aldehyde reacts faster than a ketone. Always inspect the product's four attached groups.
points: Nucleophile · Bonds to carbon · Planar → tetrahedral
C=O π pair · Moves toward O · Oxygen bears charge
Proton transfer · Completes product · Check stereochemistry

chapters.title: Reduction products depend on how far oxygen is removed
chapters.formula: R-CHO -> R-CH2OH by suitable hydride; R-CO-R' -> R-CH2-R' by compatible carbonyl deoxygenation
chapters.script: A suitable hydride reduction converts an aldehyde to a primary alcohol and a ketone to a secondary alcohol. This retains oxygen as hydroxyl. Clemmensen reduction under acidic conditions and Wolff-Kishner reduction under basic conditions instead convert a compatible carbonyl group to methylene. Choose conditions that the other functional groups can tolerate. Aldehydes are readily oxidized to carboxylic acids or their salts in common tests; ketones generally resist these mild oxidations. Tollens' silver-mirror response supports an oxidizable substrate, but is not uniquely diagnostic of every aldehyde: some other reducing compounds respond too. Ordinary ketones are usually negative, while alpha-hydroxy ketones are an important exception. Consider acetone. Hydride reduction gives isopropyl alcohol with three carbons and oxygen still present. Complete carbonyl deoxygenation instead gives propane with three carbons and no oxygen in the organic product. Tollens oxidation is another change: acetaldehyde gives an acetate product under the basic test conditions. Acid work-up changes the protonation state, so do not confuse a carboxylate salt with an uncharged acid.
points: Hydride reduction · Isopropyl alcohol · Yes, as OH
Deoxygenation · Propane · No
Mild aldehyde tests · Ordinary ketone resists · Check exceptions

chapters.title: Alpha hydrogen opens an aldol pathway
chapters.formula: 2 CH3CHO -> CH3CH(OH)CH2CHO; dehydration -> CH3CH=CHCHO + H2O
chapters.script: Hydrogen on a carbon adjacent to a carbonyl is an alpha hydrogen. Removing it with a suitable base produces an enolate stabilized by resonance. In an aldol addition, this carbon nucleophile attacks another carbonyl molecule to form a beta-hydroxy carbonyl product. Dehydration can then give an alpha,beta-unsaturated product. acetaldehyde gives three hydroxybutanal in its simple self-aldol addition, and heating can produce but two enal. Benzaldehyde has no alpha hydrogen, so it cannot undergo the same self-aldol route. With concentrated hydroxide it can undergo Cannizzaro disproportionation, giving benzoate and benzyl alcohol. Lack of alpha hydrogen distinguishes the elementary pathways; crossed reactions require more careful analysis. Carbon counting is a strong check. Two molecules of the two carbon aldehyde combine to give a four carbon aldol product. The initial addition retains all the oxygen and hydrogen atoms overall; later dehydration removes water and introduces a double bond. In Cannizzaro chemistry, one aldehyde molecule is oxidized while another is reduced. It is disproportionation, not a carbon chain doubling reaction.
points: Acetaldehyde · Yes · Self-aldol possible
Benzaldehyde · No · Cannizzaro possible
Aldol addition · 2 C + 2 C · 4-carbon product

chapters.title: The iodoform test asks about a structural pattern
chapters.formula: Iodoform pattern: CH3CO- or a precursor oxidizable to it under the test conditions
chapters.script: Methyl ketones contain a methyl carbonyl group and can give yellow iodoform with iodine and base. Alcohols oxidizable to that pattern can also respond, as can ethanol through acetaldehyde. isopropyl alcohol is positive; one propanol normally is not. Therefore a positive result does not prove the original sample was already a ketone. Do not combine test rules blindly. acetaldehyde is both an aldehyde and an iodoform-positive compound; benzaldehyde can give Tollens' response but lacks the methyl-carbonyl pattern. Carbonyl derivative formation helps establish a carbonyl group but does not alone distinguish every aldehyde from every ketone.  Acetone contains a methyl group directly attached to its carbonyl carbon and is a standard positive example. Diethyl ketone lacks that methyl ketone arrangement and is ordinarily negative. Compare the carbonyl carbon's immediate neighbours rather than looking for a methyl group anywhere in the molecule. Use more than one observation for identification, since one positive response can correspond to several functional groups or precursors.
points: Acetone · Positive · Methyl ketone
Isopropyl alcohol · Positive · Oxidizes to acetone
1-Propanol · Usually negative · No required precursor

board.heading: The iodoform test asks about a structural pattern

chapters.title: Carboxylic acid strength depends on the surroundings
chapters.formula: R-COOH + HCO3- -> R-COO- + CO2 + H2O
chapters.script: Carboxylic acids can release carbon dioxide from bicarbonate, helping distinguish them from ordinary phenols and alcohols. Their conjugate bases are resonance-stabilized carboxylates. An electron-withdrawing substituent generally stabilizes nearby negative charge and increases acidity, with an inductive effect that weakens as the substituent becomes more distant. For comparable aqueous conditions, chloroacetic acid is stronger than acetic acid because chlorine withdraws electron density. Acid-catalysed esterification with an alcohol is reversible, so composition and water removal affect yield. Exam answers should track functional groups, reagent conditions and carbon count before applying an isolated reaction name. Chlorine's inductive effect is strongest when it lies near the carboxyl group and diminishes with separation along the chain. Replacing a chlorine substituent by a different group requires a fresh comparison rather than a universal ranking by atom count. In esterification, an acid and alcohol supply the two carbon portions of the ester. Acetic acid plus ethanol gives a four carbon ester and water under suitable equilibrium conditions.
points: Chloroacetic acid · Electron withdrawal · Stronger than acetic
Distant substituent · Weaker induction · Smaller effect
Acid + alcohol · Esterification · Reversible reaction

chapters.title: Ethers: synthesis and cleavage
chapters.formula: Ar–O–CH₃ + HI → Ar–OH + CH₃I under suitable conditions
chapters.script: An ether links two carbon groups through oxygen. In Williamson synthesis, an alkoxide attacks a suitable alkyl halide by backside substitution. A primary electrophile is usually preferred because increasing crowding can favour elimination rather than the desired substitution. To prepare ethyl tert butyl ether conceptually, using tert butoxide with an appropriate ethyl halide is more suitable than asking ethoxide to displace a leaving group at a tertiary carbon. The same product formula does not make both proposed routes equally effective. Strong hydrogen halides can cleave appropriate ethers after oxygen protonation. With an aryl methyl ether, cleavage at the methyl side can give methyl halide and phenol; ordinary backside attack does not simply displace oxygen at an aromatic carbon. For anisole with suitable hydrogen iodide conditions, the conceptual products are phenol and methyl iodide. Cleavage extent and products depend on substrate, reagent amount and conditions. Distinguish ether cleavage from aromatic ring substitution, and check which carbon oxygen bond actually breaks before drawing the products.

chapters.title: Carbonyl synthesis and carbon accounting
chapters.formula: Carbonyl carbon + Grignard carbon group → new C–C bond
chapters.script: A Grignard reagent contributes a carbon group to a suitable carbonyl compound. After the addition stage, protonation of the oxygen gives an alcohol. Keep the carbonyl carbon in the product and attach the incoming group to it. Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, other simple aldehydes give secondary alcohols, and ketones give tertiary alcohols under suitable conditions. For methylmagnesium bromide and formaldehyde, one incoming carbon joins one carbonyl carbon, giving a two carbon primary alcohol after work-up. With acetaldehyde, the same methyl reagent gives a three carbon secondary alcohol, isopropyl alcohol. With acetone, it gives a four carbon tertiary alcohol, tert butyl alcohol. These products demonstrate that alcohol classification depends on the final carbon carrying oxygen. A molecule containing an acidic proton can quench the reagent before addition, so a carboxylic acid cannot be treated like an uncharged ketone in this prediction. Identify incompatible groups and the order of addition before using a carbon counting shortcut.

chapters.title: Choose a reduction by functional group
chapters.formula: Carbonyl reduction preserves the carbon skeleton
chapters.script: A reducing agent must be chosen for the actual functional group. In the ordinary introductory comparison, sodium borohydride reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols. Formaldehyde gives methanol; acetaldehyde gives ethanol; acetone gives the secondary alcohol isopropyl alcohol. The carbonyl carbon remains in the product, so no carbon is added by this reduction. A suitable lithium aluminium hydride reduction followed by workup can also convert a carboxylic acid into a primary alcohol. Ethanoic acid therefore gives ethanol while retaining its two carbons. Do not assign this ordinary acid reduction to sodium borohydride merely because both reagents contain hydrogen. Reagent selectivity and the workup are part of the stated transformation. Reduction of a ketone creates a secondary alcohol, whereas reduction of an aldehyde other than formaldehyde creates a primary alcohol. A carbonyl attached to different substituents can also create a new stereogenic centre after reduction, so a flat formula alone may not describe all stereochemical products. Start with functional class, check reagent scope, then verify the carbon count and final oxygen bonding.
points: Aldehyde · NaBH₄ reduction · Primary alcohol
Ketone · NaBH₄ reduction · Secondary alcohol
Carboxylic acid · Suitable LiAlH₄; workup · Primary alcohol; same C

chapters.title: Use chemical tests as combined evidence
chapters.formula: A test result supports a functional-group hypothesis, not a unique structure
chapters.script: Chemical tests are useful when their scope and exceptions are understood. In common introductory examples, aldehydes can reduce Tollens reagent while ordinary ketones do not. Some other reducing structures, including suitable alpha hydroxy ketones, can also respond, so a positive result is not a unique molecular identification. Two four dinitrophenylhydrazine tests for many aldehyde and ketone carbonyl groups through derivative formation; it does not by itself distinguish the two classes. The iodoform test instead points to a methyl ketone or a structure that can form the required intermediate under the test conditions. Ethanol and isopropyl alcohol are familiar positive alcohol examples, whereas ordinary propyl alcohol is negative in the standard comparison. A ferric chloride colour response can support a phenolic group but is not a universal proof of one particular phenol. Combine observations with the molecular formula and other evidence. Never infer a complete structure from one colour or precipitate alone. These are principles for interpreting supplied observations, rather than instructions for carrying out laboratory tests.
points: 2,4-DNPH · Many aldehydes / ketones · Does not separate classes
Tollens · Reducing structures · Ordinary ketones negative
Iodoform · Methyl-ketone pathway · Ethanol also positive

chapters.title: Phenol formylation and carboxylation
chapters.formula: Reimer–Tiemann adds CHO; Kolbe–Schmitt adds COOH after workup
chapters.script: Two named phenol transformations add a carbon but give different functional groups. In the standard Reimer Tiemann reaction, phenol with chloroform and aqueous base followed by the stated workup gives mainly an ortho formyl product. The familiar product is salicylaldehyde, also called two hydroxybenzaldehyde. Its new group is an aldehyde, not a carboxylic acid. In the Kolbe Schmitt transformation, a phenoxide reacts with carbon dioxide under appropriate conditions and acid workup gives salicylic acid, or two hydroxybenzoic acid, as the familiar main product. Here the new carbon belongs to a carboxyl group. Both products have seven carbons compared with phenol's six, but they differ in oxidation level and functional class. The directing pattern is a useful introductory outcome, not a claim that no other positional product can ever form. Keep the reagent source of the added carbon visible in a reaction map. Chloroform and carbon dioxide are not interchangeable labels. Identify the new group first, then name the product and count the ring plus substituent carbons.
points: Reimer–Tiemann · CHCl₃ / base; workup · Salicylaldehyde; CHO
Kolbe–Schmitt · Phenoxide + CO₂; workup · Salicylic acid; COOH

chapters.title: Aldol condensation versus disproportionation
chapters.formula: Alpha H permits aldol; absence of alpha H can permit Cannizzaro
chapters.script: Aldol and Cannizzaro questions require inspecting the carbon next to the carbonyl. Acetaldehyde has alpha hydrogens and can form an enolate under suitable base conditions. Two molecules first give a four carbon hydroxy aldehyde with formula C H three, C H with O H, C H two, C H O. Subsequent dehydration gives the unsaturated aldehyde commonly called crotonaldehyde, with four carbons still present. Water loss does not remove a carbon. Benzaldehyde lacks an alpha hydrogen at its carbonyl substituent, so it does not undergo that ordinary self aldol pathway. Under suitable concentrated base conditions, two benzaldehyde molecules can instead disproportionate through the Cannizzaro reaction. One becomes benzyl alcohol and the other a benzoate ion. Each organic product retains seven carbons; the two molecules have not joined into one fourteen carbon product. Acid workup converts benzoate to benzoic acid. State whether the question asks for the initial addition product, the dehydrated product or the material after workup. These choices change the formula and functional groups even when the carbon accounting remains straightforward.
points: Acetaldehyde · Alpha H present · CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CHO
Aldol dehydration · Lose H₂O · Crotonaldehyde; still 4 C
Benzaldehyde · No alpha H; strong base · Alcohol + benzoate; 7 C each

chapters.title: Calculate an esterification equilibrium
chapters.formula: For the supplied ideal model: K = x²/(1 − x)²
chapters.script: Esterification is reversible, so a catalyst does not guarantee complete conversion. Consider an illustrative homogeneous ideal equilibrium model for one mole of ethanoic acid and one mole of ethanol, initially without ester or water. The balanced reaction forms one mole each of ethyl ethanoate and water for every mole of acid consumed. Let the extent in moles be x. Remaining acid and alcohol are each one minus x, while ester and water are each x. For a supplied equilibrium constant of four in this ideal ratio model, the square of x divided by the square of the quantity one minus x equals four. Take the positive square root to obtain x divided by one minus x equals two. Solving gives x equal to two thirds, so about sixty six point seven percent of each starting reactant is converted. Check that every amount stays nonnegative and the quotient returns four. Actual mixtures need their appropriate activities and conditions. A catalyst speeds approach to equilibrium at fixed temperature without changing its constant. Removing a product can alter the equilibrium composition.
points: Initial acid / alcohol · 1.00 mol each · No initial ester / water
Equilibrium amounts · 1−x, 1−x, x, x · K = x²/(1−x)²
Supplied K = 4 · x/(1−x) = 2 · x = 2/3 mol

chapters.title: Mixed aldol reactions need donor and acceptor choices
chapters.formula: Two enolizable carbonyl partners can give two self and two crossed connectivities
chapters.script: An aldol question has two roles: an enolate donor and a carbonyl acceptor. If acetaldehyde and propionaldehyde are mixed under an idealized ordinary base catalyzed aldol model, both have alpha hydrogens and can supply enolate donors. Each donor can attack either aldehyde. The elementary first addition list therefore has two self aldol connectivities and two crossed connectivities, four in total. Acetaldehyde acting as donor and propionaldehyde as acceptor is not the same connectivity as propionaldehyde donating to acetaldehyde, because the carbonyl group retained in the product belongs to the donor. Stereoisomers and later dehydration products can enlarge a more detailed product list. Thus four is a restricted connectivity count, not a complete description of every species present after unrestricted reaction. Benzaldehyde has no alpha hydrogen at its aldehyde side chain and cannot supply the ordinary enolate in this comparison. Pairing it with a suitable enolizable carbonyl can reduce the donor choices, but selectivity still depends on the specified conditions. Identify which partner donates, which carbonyl is attacked and whether the question asks for addition or condensation before drawing a single preferred product.
points: Acetaldehyde + propionaldehyde · Both supply enolate donors · 2 donor choices
Each donor chooses acceptor · Self or crossed addition · 4 first-addition connectivities
Benzaldehyde comparison · No aldehyde alpha hydrogen · Not the ordinary enolate donor

chapters.title: Ester hydrolysis has different acid and base accounting
chapters.formula: CH₃COOC₂H₅ + OH⁻ → CH₃COO⁻ + C₂H₅OH
chapters.script: Ester hydrolysis should distinguish an acid catalyzed equilibrium from a base promoted net conversion. For ethyl ethanoate, acid catalyzed hydrolysis connects the ester and water with ethanoic acid and ethanol. The catalyst changes the route and rate, but not the equilibrium constant at a fixed temperature. In the basic net equation, hydroxide is consumed and the acid derived product remains mainly carboxylate under the stated basic conditions. One mole of this simple ester consumes one mole hydroxide to give one mole ethanoate and one mole ethanol. Suppose an illustrative mixture contains zero point zero two zero zero mole ester and zero point zero one five zero mole hydroxide, and assume this net reaction reaches the stated stoichiometric endpoint with no competing processes. Hydroxide limits conversion to zero point zero one five zero mole. Ester remaining is zero point zero zero five zero zero mole, and ethanol formed is zero point zero one five zero mole. Do not describe hydroxide as a recovered acid catalyst in that balance. The carboxylate is not the isolated neutral acid unless a separate acidification is specified. This calculation concerns chemical accounting rather than a practical preparation.

chapters.title: Cyanohydrin addition changes carbon count and chirality
chapters.formula: CH₃CHO + HCN ⇌ CH₃CH(OH)CN: one new carbon
chapters.script: A carbonyl addition product can introduce both a new carbon and a stereochemical question. In cyanohydrin formation, the cyanide carbon forms a bond to the carbonyl carbon, followed by proton transfer to oxygen. For acetaldehyde, the product has a carbon bearing hydroxyl, hydrogen, methyl and cyano groups. These four groups differ, so the former planar carbonyl carbon becomes a stereogenic centre. In an achiral environment with no chiral influence, attack at the two enantiotopic faces gives the two enantiomers in equal amounts in the elementary model. The mixture is racemic, rather than a single assigned configuration. Acetaldehyde contributes two carbons and the cyano group one, giving three carbons overall. The corresponding propanone cyanohydrin contains two identical methyl groups at the hydroxyl bearing carbon, so that carbon is not stereogenic despite the same general addition pattern. A carbon count alone therefore cannot establish chirality. The process is reversible and its extent depends on substrate and conditions; the connectivity exercise does not assert complete conversion. Read the cyano carbon explicitly instead of confusing nucleophilic addition with replacement of an existing carbon atom.
points: Acetaldehyde cyanohydrin · H, OH, CH₃ and CN at one C · Stereogenic; 3 carbons total

chapters.title: Use supplied pKa data before ranking acid amounts
chapters.formula: Ka ratio = 10^(pKa,weak − pKa,strong)
chapters.script: Acid strength and the amount of acid in a solution answer different questions. Compare two supplied monoprotic carboxylic acids in the same solvent at the same temperature, with p K a values three and five. The lower p K a corresponds to the larger acid dissociation constant. Their constant ratio is ten squared, or one hundred, so the first acid is stronger on that defined scale. This does not mean every equal concentration solution has one hundred times the hydrogen ion concentration. Dissociation must also satisfy mass balance and any approximations used. In an ideal weak acid range, where both acids remain only slightly ionized and water ionization is negligible, hydrogen ion concentration scales approximately with the square root of K a times analytical concentration. At equal concentration, a hundredfold K a ratio would then give roughly a tenfold hydrogen ion ratio. Check the small ionization assumption for each acid before applying that estimate. Electron withdrawing substituents can stabilize a carboxylate and increase acidity, while their distance and structural position matter. Supplied same solvent data support the numerical ranking without pretending that a substituent name alone determines every measured p H.
points: Acid A pKa=3; B pKa=5 · Ka,A/Ka,B = 10² · A is 100× larger in Ka
Equal C; both weakly ionized · [H⁺] ≈ √(Ka C) · Approximate [H⁺] ratio 10

chapters.title: Carbonyl derivatives keep the carbon ledger but lose water
chapters.formula: R₂C=O + NH₂OH ⇌ R₂C=N–OH + H₂O
chapters.script: Aldehydes and ketones can form nitrogen containing derivatives by condensation with suitable nitrogen nucleophiles. Hydroxylamine gives an oxime, replacing the carbonyl double bond with a carbon nitrogen double bond while retaining an oxygen hydrogen group on nitrogen. Hydrazine gives a hydrazone with a carbon nitrogen double bond and an N H two group attached to that nitrogen. In each simple net equation, one water molecule is eliminated per carbonyl group converted. For acetone plus hydroxylamine, the product oxime has three carbons, seven hydrogens, one nitrogen and one oxygen. Acetone plus hydrazine instead gives the corresponding hydrazone with three carbons, eight hydrogens and two nitrogens. No carbon has been added by either nitrogen reagent. Acetone's two identical methyl groups also mean its simple oxime does not give a distinct E and Z pair at the carbon nitrogen bond. An unsymmetrical carbonyl derivative may require a geometrical isomerism check. Formation and hydrolysis depend on conditions; these net equations do not mean every mixture converts completely. Count the reagent atoms and eliminated water before assigning a derivative formula.

chapters.title: Phenol bromination depends on the reaction medium
chapters.formula: C₆H₅OH + 3Br₂ → C₆H₂Br₃OH + 3HBr
chapters.script: Phenol's hydroxyl group strongly activates its ring toward electrophilic substitution and favours ortho and para positions. In the standard introductory bromine water comparison, phenol can form two four six tribromophenol, with three ring hydrogens replaced by bromine. The net equation uses three bromine molecules for each phenol and produces three hydrogen bromide units. The oxygen hydrogen bond is retained in this ring substitution ledger. With phenol molar mass ninety four and bromine atom mass eighty, the tribrominated product has molar mass three hundred thirty one grams per mole, because three hydrogens of mass one are replaced by three bromines. Thus zero point zero one zero zero mole product has theoretical mass three point three one grams using those supplied values. Under different controlled low polarity conditions, monobromination can instead be favoured, commonly giving ortho and para products. Do not transfer the three bromine stoichiometry into every phenol bromination question without reading the stated medium and extent. A precipitate observation supports a reaction pattern, not a unique identification of every unknown phenolic sample.

chapters.title: Carboxylate carbon loss can give different alkane sizes
chapters.formula: Soda-lime model: n→n−1 C; Kolbe coupling: n→2(n−1) C
chapters.script: Two carboxylate transformations can lose the carboxyl carbon yet give different hydrocarbon sizes. In the standard soda lime decarboxylation model, sodium propanoate gives ethane: the three carbon salt loses its carboxyl carbon into carbonate, leaving a two carbon hydrocarbon. A balanced net equation combines sodium propanoate and sodium hydroxide to form ethane and sodium carbonate. In the ideal Kolbe electrolysis comparison, two propanoate ions each lose one electron and one carbon dioxide unit at the anode. The resulting two ethyl radicals couple to form butane, a four carbon molecule. The anodic net equation is two propanoate ions forming butane, two carbon dioxide molecules and two electrons. One mole of coupled butane therefore corresponds to two moles of electrons in that ideal anodic model. This is a carbon and charge ledger, not a statement that electrolysis always gives a single product at full efficiency. Competing reactions and substrate structure can affect the actual product mixture. Distinguish these transformations from the Kolbe Schmitt carboxylation of phenoxide, which has a similar name but adds a carboxyl group to an aromatic system.

chapters.title: Ester aminolysis replaces the acyl substituent
chapters.formula: CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NH₃ → CH₃CONH₂ + C₂H₅OH
chapters.script: An ester can react with ammonia under suitable conditions to give an amide and an alcohol. In the simple ethyl ethanoate example, the acyl fragment contains two carbons and the ethoxy fragment contains two more. Aminolysis produces ethanamide from the two carbon acyl fragment and ethanol from the two carbon ethoxy fragment. The total carbon count remains four across the two organic products. The net equation consumes one ammonia per ester and does not eliminate water in this ester to amide accounting. That differs from writing a direct carboxylic acid plus ammonia condensation without considering initial salt formation or conditions. In the usual nucleophilic acyl substitution description, ammonia attacks the carbonyl carbon, a tetrahedral intermediate forms, proton transfers occur and the alcohol-derived group departs. This is not ordinary backside displacement at the ethyl carbon. A neutral amide product contains a carbonyl bonded to nitrogen, while the alcohol retains the ester alkoxy oxygen in this simple unlabelled structural ledger. Reaction rate, competing hydrolysis and conversion depend on the actual ester and conditions; the net equation alone supplies stoichiometry.

quiz.question: Oxidation of a simple secondary alcohol with a suitable oxidant gives:
quiz.explanation: The carbon bearing OH becomes a carbonyl carbon with its two carbon substituents retained.

quiz.question: The ordinary major site of nucleophilic attack in a simple carbonyl group is:
quiz.explanation: Bond polarization makes the carbonyl carbon electrophilic, so a nucleophile forms a bond there.

quiz.question: Which lacks an alpha hydrogen for the usual self-aldol reaction?
quiz.explanation: Benzaldehyde's CHO group is attached directly to the ring and has no adjacent alpha C-H site.

quiz.question: A standard positive iodoform test is expected for:
quiz.explanation: Propan-2-ol oxidizes to propanone, which contains the required methyl-ketone pattern.

quiz.question: Which ordinarily releases CO2 with aqueous bicarbonate?
quiz.explanation: A carboxylic acid protonates bicarbonate, forming carbon dioxide and water in the usual test.

quiz.question: The first self-aldol addition product of ethanal is:
quiz.explanation: Initial addition gives the beta-hydroxy aldehyde; dehydration is a separate further transformation.

quiz.question: Williamson ether synthesis is usually best planned using:
options: A tertiary electrophile in every case
Only an aryl chloride under ordinary SN2 conditions
quiz.explanation: An accessible primary centre favours backside substitution; tertiary electrophiles often eliminate.

quiz.question: Suitable HI cleavage of anisole gives the conceptual products:
quiz.explanation: Cleavage occurs at the methyl side rather than by ordinary backside displacement at aromatic carbon.

quiz.question: Methylmagnesium bromide plus acetone, followed by suitable work-up, gives:
quiz.explanation: The incoming methyl adds one carbon to acetone, giving tert-butyl alcohol.

quiz.question: Which change retains oxygen as OH in the organic product?
options: Ether cleavage to two alkenes necessarily
Acetone hydride reduction to isopropyl alcohol
quiz.explanation: Hydride reduction converts C=O into the alcohol group while retaining oxygen.

quiz.question: Ordinary NaBH4 reduction of acetone gives:
quiz.explanation: A ketone reduces to a secondary alcohol while retaining its three-carbon skeleton.

quiz.question: A positive 2,4-DNPH result alone normally establishes:
options: Evidence for a suitable aldehyde or ketone carbonyl
That every ketone reduces Tollens reagent
quiz.explanation: The derivative test supports carbonyl-class identification but does not alone distinguish aldehyde from ketone.

quiz.question: The familiar principal Reimer–Tiemann product from phenol is:
quiz.explanation: The transformation introduces a formyl group; the usual ortho product is salicylaldehyde.

quiz.question: Two benzaldehyde molecules in a suitable Cannizzaro reaction produce:
quiz.explanation: One aldehyde is reduced and one oxidized; each main organic product retains seven carbons.

quiz.question: In the stated ideal esterification model, initial acid/alcohol are 1 mol each and K=4. Extent x is:
quiz.explanation: x/(1−x)=2 gives 3x=2; substitution returns K=4.

quiz.question: The familiar Kolbe–Schmitt product after acid workup is:
quiz.explanation: Carbon dioxide supplies the new carboxyl carbon in the phenol-derived acid.

quiz.question: Acetaldehyde and propionaldehyde both provide enolate donors. Counting only elementary first aldol addition connectivities gives:
quiz.explanation: Two donor choices times two acceptor choices gives two self and two crossed connectivities, excluding stereoisomers and later reactions.

quiz.question: In a crossed aldol addition, the carbonyl group retained before dehydration belongs to the:
quiz.explanation: The donor enolate re-forms its carbonyl while the acceptor carbonyl becomes the alcohol-bearing site.

quiz.question: In base-promoted ethyl ethanoate hydrolysis, the immediate acid-derived species under basic conditions is:
quiz.explanation: The net reaction consumes hydroxide and forms the carboxylate plus ethanol.

quiz.question: 0.0200 mol simple ester meets 0.0150 mol hydroxide. At the stipulated complete 1:1 net endpoint, ester remaining is:
quiz.explanation: Hydroxide limits conversion to 0.0150 mol; subtract this from the initial ester amount.

quiz.question: Acetaldehyde cyanohydrin contains how many carbon atoms?
quiz.explanation: Two carbons originate in acetaldehyde and one is supplied by the cyano carbon.

quiz.question: Under the elementary achiral model, acetaldehyde cyanohydrin is formed as:
options: An achiral carbon with two methyl groups
quiz.explanation: The new carbon has four different groups, and equal attack on the two enantiotopic faces gives a racemate.

quiz.question: Acids A and B have pKa 3 and 5 at matching conditions. Ka,A/Ka,B is:
quiz.explanation: Ka=10^(−pKa), so the ratio is 10^(5−3)=100.

quiz.question: Only when both equal-concentration acids satisfy the small-ionization model, that Ka ratio predicts an approximate hydrogen-ion ratio of:
quiz.explanation: The weak-acid approximation gives hydrogen-ion concentration proportional to sqrt(Ka C), so sqrt(100)=10.

quiz.question: Acetone plus hydroxylamine forms the simple oxime with net loss of:
quiz.explanation: Oxime condensation replaces C=O with C=N–OH and eliminates one water molecule in the simple net equation.

quiz.question: Acetone has formula C3H6O. Its simple hydrazone from N2H4 has formula:
quiz.explanation: Add N2H4 to C3H6O and subtract H2O; the result is C3H8N2 with no added carbon.

quiz.question: Using phenol M=94, Br=80 and H=1, molar mass of 2,4,6-tribromophenol is:
quiz.explanation: Three ring hydrogens are replaced: 94−3×1+3×80=331 g/mol.

quiz.question: Under the stated tribromination model, phenol consumes bromine molecules per molecule in ratio:
quiz.explanation: Each of three ring substitutions consumes one Br2 and releases one HBr, so one phenol uses three Br2.

quiz.question: Sodium propanoate has three carbons. In the standard soda-lime decarboxylation model its hydrocarbon is:
quiz.explanation: The carboxyl carbon is removed from the organic skeleton, leaving the two-carbon ethane product.

quiz.question: Ideal Kolbe coupling of two propanoate ions instead gives:
quiz.explanation: Each propanoate loses its carboxyl carbon to give an ethyl radical; two two-carbon radicals couple to butane.

quiz.question: Ethyl ethanoate aminolysis with ammonia gives:
quiz.explanation: Ammonia replaces the alcohol-derived group at the acyl centre; the two carbon fragments become ethanamide and ethanol.

quiz.question: In that simple ester aminolysis net equation, the number of water molecules eliminated per ester is:
quiz.explanation: The net products are an amide and an alcohol; no water is eliminated in this ester-to-amide atom ledger.
